Newborn Care

Postpartum thyroiditis: changing symptoms, recovery and follow-up

Updated: October 19, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Exhaustion, changes in mood and a racing heart after birth deserve attention. Sometimes thyroid inflammation contributes, but symptoms alone cannot identify the cause. Postpartum thyroiditis is an autoimmune condition during the first year after birth. Its course varies, so assessment and follow-up matter more than expecting everyone to pass through the same stages.

What postpartum thyroiditis means

The thyroid is a small gland at the front of the neck that makes hormones involved in energy use and many body functions. In postpartum thyroiditis, inflammation can release stored hormone into the bloodstream, followed by a period of reduced hormone production. This is usually painless and is different from Graves’ disease, which causes excess hormone production.

The condition is linked to autoimmune activity changing after pregnancy. Antibodies against thyroid tissue are often present, with similarities to Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. It can also occur after pregnancy loss or in someone with existing autoimmune thyroid disease; previously normal thyroid tests do not rule it out.

A possible early high-hormone phase

Anxiety, irritability, a fast or noticeable heartbeat, unexplained weight loss, heat intolerance, tiredness, tremor and difficulty sleeping can occur when stored hormone is released. These are not specific to thyroid disease, and tiredness can occur in either phase. Do not assume that palpitations or weight change are simply part of looking after a baby.

This phase often begins within about one to six months after birth and may last weeks to a few months. Some people notice little or no high-hormone phase. Timing helps the assessment but cannot confirm the diagnosis or distinguish it reliably from other thyroid conditions.

A possible later low-hormone phase

Low energy, feeling unusually cold, constipation, dry skin, weight gain and low mood can occur when hormone production falls. This often becomes apparent around four to eight months after birth and can last several months. Symptoms can affect daily life even when they seem similar to sleep deprivation or ordinary postpartum changes.

Some people have only the low phase, some only the high phase and some both. There is no compulsory sequence or fixed gap between them. A change in symptoms after an earlier reassuring result is a reason to contact the clinician again rather than assuming the thyroid must still be working normally.

Who should discuss a monitoring plan

Risk is higher with a previous episode of postpartum thyroiditis, thyroid antibodies, a personal history of thyroid dysfunction, another autoimmune condition such as type 1 diabetes, or a family history of thyroid disease. Having one of these factors does not mean the condition will definitely develop, and absence of a known risk factor does not exclude it.

Tell the maternity or primary-care team about these conditions during pregnancy or after birth. Agree whether and when thyroid blood tests are needed and whom to contact for new symptoms. A previous episode also matters when planning another pregnancy because recurrence is possible; a single percentage cannot predict an individual’s course.

Symptoms, blood tests and mood need assessment together

A clinician considers the symptom pattern, examination, pregnancy and thyroid history, and medicines or supplements. TSH and thyroid hormone measurements help show current function; antibodies or other tests may be useful in selected circumstances. Distinguishing postpartum thyroiditis from Graves’ disease matters because their treatments differ. Not everyone needs a scan or the same set of tests.

Low mood, anxiety and poor sleep may coexist with thyroid dysfunction, postpartum depression or other problems. The 2026 ATA review did not establish a consistent association between postpartum thyroiditis and postpartum depression. Thyroid testing follows clinical indications; mental-health support should not wait for a blood result. Normal thyroid tests do not make distress less real or remove the need for care.

Treatment depends on the phase and your circumstances

Mild symptoms may need monitoring rather than medicine. A clinician may prescribe a suitable beta-blocker briefly for troublesome high-phase symptoms. Antithyroid medicines do not treat hormone leaking from an inflamed gland; this does not mean that someone treated for Graves’ disease should stop their medicine. Do not start, stop or change thyroid or heart medicines yourself.

During the low phase, levothyroxine may be considered according to symptoms, test results, breastfeeding and plans for pregnancy, particularly within the next six months. It can usually be used while breastfeeding with professional advice; treatment is not a guaranteed milk-supply remedy. Review every medicine and supplement with the prescriber. If low thyroid function is monitored without treatment, repeat blood tests are commonly arranged in four to eight weeks, with timing individualized.

Recovery does not remove the need for follow-up

Many people recover thyroid function within roughly 12–18 months of symptoms starting, but this is not a deadline or guarantee. Some remain underactive and need ongoing treatment; others recover initially but develop hypothyroidism later. Persistent symptoms need reassessment rather than waiting until the end of an expected recovery window.

Arrange the agreed blood-test follow-up even when you feel better. The 2026 ATA guideline advises checking thyroid function again one year after it normalizes, or earlier if symptoms return. Further monitoring depends on history and results. If levothyroxine was started, a supervised reduction or stopping trial may be appropriate later, but not independently or automatically when planning pregnancy. Discuss pregnancy plans early so thyroid function and treatment can be reviewed.

Prevention and everyday support

There is no guaranteed way to prevent postpartum thyroiditis. Routine levothyroxine or selenium supplements are not recommended just to prevent it. Do not use extra iodine, kelp or a ‘thyroid support’ product as a substitute for assessment; discuss supplements and any nutritional needs with the care team.

Record changing symptoms, medicines and test dates, and ask for practical help with rest and baby care. These measures support care but cannot correct a hormone disorder on their own. Seek help for persistent or troublesome symptoms instead of blaming yourself or dismissing them as the inevitable strain of parenthood.

When symptoms need urgent help

Seek assessment for recurring palpitations, persistent unexplained fatigue, weight or temperature intolerance changes, or mood symptoms affecting daily life. Ask promptly for mental-health support if distress worsens or coping is difficult. Possible postpartum psychosis (such as hallucinations, delusional beliefs, marked confusion or unusually elevated, overactive behaviour) needs urgent same-day assessment.

Use immediate emergency care for palpitations that do not settle, or palpitations with chest pain, breathlessness, feeling faint, fainting or loss of consciousness. Immediate danger of harm to yourself or the baby also needs emergency help. Do not drive yourself or wait for thyroid tests, an app record or a routine appointment when emergency symptoms are present.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Describe when symptoms began after pregnancy, how they have changed and your personal or family thyroid and autoimmune history. Ask which tests and follow-up fit your situation.

Agree phase-appropriate care, a repeat-test plan and medicine advice that considers breastfeeding and future pregnancy. Do not self-adjust treatment or use a supplement as a thyroid remedy.

Seek mental-health help alongside physical assessment when needed. Use urgent or emergency care for warning symptoms without waiting for test results or tracking.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help record changing symptoms, medicines, blood-test dates and appointment questions. It cannot diagnose thyroiditis, distinguish its phases or assess an emergency. Warning symptoms take priority over tracking.

When to seek help

Do not dismiss persistent symptoms as ordinary postpartum tiredness or change medicines yourself. Possible postpartum psychosis needs urgent same-day assessment. Palpitations that persist, or with chest pain, breathlessness, feeling faint, fainting or loss of consciousness, and immediate danger of harm to yourself or the baby need immediate emergency help. Do not drive yourself or wait for thyroid testing.

Evidence notes updated: October 19, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Postpartum thyroiditis can cause a high phase, a low phase or both during the first year after birth.
  • Autoimmune and thyroid history help identify risk; symptoms and properly interpreted tests guide care.
  • Recovery varies, and repeat testing matters after improvement and before another pregnancy.
  • Mood problems need support in their own right; cardiac warning symptoms or immediate danger need emergency help.

Frequently asked questions

What is postpartum thyroiditis?

It is autoimmune thyroid inflammation in the first year after birth. Stored hormone may leak out initially, and hormone production may later fall. Not everyone has both phases. It can also occur after pregnancy loss or alongside existing autoimmune thyroid disease.

What symptoms can it cause?

The high phase can bring anxiety, irritability, a racing heart, unexplained weight loss, heat intolerance, tiredness, tremor and insomnia. The low phase can bring low energy, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, weight gain and low mood. Symptoms alone cannot establish a thyroid diagnosis.

Why does it happen?

It is associated with autoimmune changes after pregnancy and often with antibodies against thyroid tissue. Prior postpartum thyroiditis, other thyroid disease, type 1 diabetes or another autoimmune condition, thyroid antibodies and family history can increase risk. It is not a failure to cope with baby care.

What complications are possible?

Some people remain hypothyroid and need ongoing treatment; others recover but develop underactive thyroid function later. Many recover within about 12–18 months from symptom onset, but this is not guaranteed. Agreed follow-up and early review before another pregnancy remain important.

Does low mood mean I need thyroid treatment?

No. Thyroid dysfunction and postpartum mental-health conditions can have overlapping symptoms or coexist. Assessment determines whether thyroid tests or treatment are appropriate. Seek mental-health support without waiting for a thyroid result, including when tests are normal.

Can I be treated while breastfeeding?

Suitable treatment is often possible. A prescriber may select a beta-blocker for troublesome high-phase symptoms or levothyroxine for low thyroid function, according to circumstances. Tell the team you are breastfeeding and discuss all medicines; do not change treatment yourself or assume it will increase milk supply.

Can I prevent it or stop treatment once I feel better?

There is no guaranteed prevention, and routine selenium or thyroid hormone is not recommended solely to prevent it. Improvement does not establish recovery. Keep the test plan; any levothyroxine reduction or stopping trial needs supervision and consideration of pregnancy plans.

Which symptoms must not wait for a thyroid appointment?

Palpitations that do not settle, or with chest pain, breathlessness, feeling faint, fainting or loss of consciousness need immediate emergency care. So does immediate danger of harm to yourself or the baby. Possible hallucinations, delusions, marked confusion or unusually elevated overactive behaviour after birth need urgent same-day assessment. Do not drive yourself in an emergency.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
